nameStory: The brown-lipped snail gets its name from the distinctive brown or dark rim around the opening of its shell, called the aperture. This brown 'lip' is like nature's signature, helping distinguish it from its close cousin, the white-lipped snail. It's also called the grove snail because it loves hanging out in wooded groves and gardens.
description: The brown-lipped snail is one of New England's most common large land snails, originally from Europe but now well-established here. Its round, dome-shaped shell comes in a rainbow of colors - yellow, pink, brown, or white - often decorated with up to five dark spiral bands that can be thick, thin, or completely absent. The shell typically measures about an inch across when fully grown. Like all land snails, it carries its home on its back and extends two pairs of tentacles when moving - the longer pair has eyes at the tips.

idTips.label: Brown lip around shell opening
idTips.description: Look for the telltale brown or dark rim around the shell's opening where the snail emerges - this lip feels smooth and hard to the touch and is usually clearly visible even on empty shells

idTips.label: Variable shell colors and banding
idTips.description: Shell can be yellow, pink, brown, or white with zero to five dark spiral bands - the bands may be complete rings or broken into segments, creating endless pattern combinations

idTips.label: Rounded, globe-like shell
idTips.description: Shell feels sturdy and smooth, shaped like a low dome or globe rather than tall and pointed - about as wide as it is tall when viewed from the side

idTips.label: Size and heft
idTips.description: Large for a land snail at about one inch across - empty shells feel surprisingly solid and weighty in your palm compared to smaller native snails

idTips.label: Shiny shell surface
idTips.description: Living snails have glossy, almost wet-looking shells that feel smooth to touch - dead shells may appear duller but still retain their smooth texture

habitat: Brown-lipped snails thrive in gardens, parks, woodland edges, and anywhere with limestone-rich or calcium-rich soil that helps build their shells. They love areas with leaf litter, compost piles, and dense vegetation where they can find shelter and moisture. You'll often find them around human settlements - in flower beds, vegetable gardens, and urban green spaces throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: Active snails emerge from winter hiding spots as temperatures warm, leaving silvery slime trails on sidewalks and garden paths after spring rains. This is peak time for finding both live snails and fresh empty shells.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid mornings and after summer storms - look for them climbing plant stems and walls. During dry spells, they may seal their shell openings and become dormant.
seasonality.fall: Snails are busy feeding before winter, often seen on fallen leaves and in compost areas. Empty shells become more noticeable as vegetation dies back.
seasonality.winter: Living snails hibernate under logs, stones, and leaf litter, but their durable shells remain visible and identifiable even when covered by snow.

funFact: These snails are living genetics laboratories - scientists have used them for over 60 years to study evolution in action because their shell patterns are inherited like human eye color, and you can actually track how populations change over time just by counting different color patterns in your backyard!
confusionNotes: The brown-lipped snail is most easily confused with its close relative, the white-lipped snail, which has an identical shell shape and size but sports a white or pale lip instead of brown. Memory trick: 'Brown-lipped snail has a brown lip' - check that shell opening rim and you'll know for sure!
contextualKnowledge: Though now completely at home in New England, brown-lipped snails are actually European immigrants that arrived accidentally with plants and soil shipments. They're so well-established that many people assume they're native, but they've only been here for about 150 years - a blink of an eye in snail evolutionary time.
compareHints: Brown-lipped snails differ from white-lipped snails primarily in that distinctive lip color around the shell opening - brown versus white or pale. Both species can have identical shell colors and banding patterns, making the lip color the most reliable distinguishing feature. White-lipped snails also tend to prefer slightly cooler, more northern locations, while brown-lipped snails are more heat-tolerant and common in urban areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The white-lipped snail is virtually identical to the brown-lipped snail in size, shape, and shell patterns, but the lip color is the dead giveaway - white versus dark brown or black.
